prompt: Explain why India's groundwater is under stress.
hook: The invisible resource is the one running out.

card.oneLiner: India is the world's largest user of groundwater, and in many districts water is being pumped out faster than rain can refill it.
keyPoints: Extraction outpaces natural recharge in stressed areas.
Aquifers are classified from safe to over-exploited.
Cheap pumping and cropping patterns drive demand.
Recharge and demand management can slow depletion.

framework.name: Central Ground Water Board
framework.gloss: Periodic classification of blocks as safe, semi-critical or over-exploited.

whatYouCanDo: Reward recharge structures and efficient irrigation.
Reduce water-intensive choices where alternatives exist.
card.caveats: Educational information, not professional advice. Assessment units and categories are revised periodically.

prompt: Explain how river pollution is measured and cleaned up.
hook: A river's health has a number.

card.oneLiner: River water quality is tracked with indicators such as biochemical oxygen demand and faecal coliform, and clean-up programmes target untreated sewage.
keyPoints: High organic load and bacteria signal sewage pollution.
Untreated sewage is the biggest source in most rivers.
Treatment plants and interception reduce pollution.
Restoring flow helps rivers dilute and recover.

framework.name: Central Pollution Control Board
framework.gloss: National monitoring of river water quality.

framework.name: Namami Gange Programme
framework.gloss: Mission to clean and revive the Ganga.

whatYouCanDo: Find the monitoring station nearest you.
Support sewage treatment and connection of households.
Reduce chemical runoff from homes and farms.
card.caveats: Educational information, not professional advice. Water quality varies by season and stretch.

prompt: Explain rainwater harvesting and why cities mandate it.

card.oneLiner: Rainwater harvesting captures roof or surface runoff for storage or for recharging groundwater, easing scarcity and urban flooding.
keyPoints: Harvesting can store water or recharge an aquifer.
Many local building rules require it for new construction.
It cuts runoff that would otherwise flood streets.
Systems need cleaning and maintenance to keep working.

framework.name: Model Building Bye-Laws
framework.gloss: Provisions adopted by many states and cities.

framework.name: Ministry of Housing and Urban Affairs

whatYouCanDo: Install a simple rooftop harvesting or recharge system.
Check your local byelaws for requirements and rebates.
card.caveats: Educational information, not professional advice. Design depends on rainfall, soil and space.

sources.title: Ministry of Housing and Urban Affairs

prompt: Explain why urban flooding is getting worse.
hook: Too much concrete, too little drainage.

card.oneLiner: Urban flooding results from heavy rain falling on paved surfaces with inadequate drainage, made worse by lost wetlands and building on floodplains.
keyPoints: Concrete stops water soaking into the ground.
Drains are often undersized or blocked.
Encroached lakes and wetlands can no longer absorb water.
Climate change brings heavier short bursts of rain.

framework.name: National Disaster Management Authority
framework.gloss: Guidance to cities on reducing flood risk.

framework.name: Ministry of Housing and Urban Affairs

whatYouCanDo: Keep drains clear and avoid dumping waste in them.
Protect local ponds, lakes and green spaces.
Support permeable surfaces and water-sensitive design.
card.caveats: Educational information, not professional advice. Flood risk depends on local geography and infrastructure.

sources.title: Ministry of Housing and Urban Affairs

prompt: Explain how safe drinking water is ensured and what to do when it is contaminated.
hook: Access is not the same as safety.

card.oneLiner: Drinking-water safety depends on protected sources, treatment and testing, and contamination can be reported and investigated.
keyPoints: Source protection and treatment sit at the heart of safety.
Some areas face natural contaminants such as arsenic and fluoride.
Routine testing checks for harmful bacteria and chemicals.
Complaints about unsafe water can be taken to local authorities.

framework.name: Bureau of Indian Standards
framework.gloss: The national standard for drinking water quality.

framework.name: Jal Jeevan Mission
framework.gloss: Programme to provide functional household tap connections.

whatYouCanDo: Ask for test results if you suspect contamination.
Use boiling or approved filters where supply is unsafe.
Report quality problems to the local body or jal board.
card.caveats: Educational information, not professional advice. Water quality varies and should be tested locally.
